Accrual and cash-basis accounting are two ways to track your business money. With cash-basis, you record income only when you actually receive payment and record expenses only when you pay them. It’s simple and shows how much cash you have on hand.

Accrual accounting records income when you earn it (even if the customer hasn’t paid yet) and records expenses when they happen (even if you haven’t paid them yet). That means you include money customers owe you and bills you haven’t paid yet. Accrual gives a more complete picture of your business activity over time, because it matches sales and the costs tied to them, not just when cash moves.

For day-to-day cash decisions, cash-basis can be easier. For understanding overall performance, planning, or if you have customers who pay later, accrual is usually more informative. Choose the method that fits your business size and needs.

Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when cash changes hands. If you complete a project in June but the client pays in July, accrual shows the sale in June. It also records bills when you incur them, even if you pay later. 

Cash-basis accounting records transactions only when money actually arrives or leaves. Using the same example, the sale would be recorded in July when the payment is received, and an expense shows up only when you pay the bill.

Accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing profit and what the business actually owes or is owed. Cash basis is simpler and shows real cash flow, but can hide receivables or unpaid bills. Many larger organizations use accrual for accuracy; smaller or very cash-focused businesses sometimes prefer cash basis for simplicity.

Note: this is a plain-language summary based on standard accounting practice; no external sources were consulted. If you’d like a short numerical example, I can add one.

If you get a bill today but pay later, the expense is recorded now. That way your books show what the business earned and what it owes in the period those activities occurred.

Cash-basis accounting records income and expenses only when cash is received or paid. You record a sale when you get paid and an expense when you pay the bill. It’s simpler and can be easier for very small businesses, but it can miss the full picture if you have lots of unpaid invoices or bills.

In short: accrual gives a more accurate view of business activity over time; cash-basis is easier to use but only shows money when it actually changes hands.

With accrual accounting, you record income when you earn it (even if the customer hasn’t paid yet) and record expenses when you incur them (even if you haven’t paid the bill). 

That means accrual shows invoices you’ve sent (accounts receivable) and bills you owe (accounts payable), giving a clearer picture of ongoing profit and loss over a period. Cash basis can hide those details and sometimes make results jumpy if payments are delayed. Accrual is usually preferred for understanding long-term performance or when you have credit sales or inventory; cash basis can work for very small, cash-focused businesses.
